It cannot be assumed that most health workers have recently undergone Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) training, that such training included immunization components, or that training directly translates into improved clinical practices. 2. The Integrated Community Case Management (iCCM) strategy has been adopted by many countries to enhance access to life-saving treatments for common childhood illnesses. This approach is particularly implemented in hard-to-reach areas, often defined as communities located five or more kilometers from the nearest health facility. 3. Under the iCCM strategy, community health workers (CHWs) are trained, supervised, and equipped to assess, classify, and treat conditions such as fast-breathing pneumonia with amoxicillin, malaria with artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), and diarrhea with oral rehydration salts (ORS) and zinc. They are also responsible for assessing, classifying, and referring children with severe diseases to health facilities. 4. CHWs may also engage in community mobilization for vaccinations. As part of the iCCM case-management protocol, the vaccination status of every sick child presenting to a CHW should be checked. If a child is found to be unvaccinated, the CHW is expected to take steps to ensure the child receives the necessary vaccinations. 5. Tetanus remains a significant public health issue, particularly in the poorest districts of tropical developing countries, where maternal and neonatal tetanus (MNT) dominate morbidity and mortality statistics. Tetanus is preventable through tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines (TTCVs), which are part of childhood immunization programs. However, booster doses are required for long-lasting immunity. 6. The integration of TTCV vaccination for pregnant women within antenatal care (ANC) is a long-standing practice. Women of reproductive age are also targeted during immunization campaigns in high-risk districts for MNT, providing an opportunity to deliver other interventions simultaneously. 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a minimum of eight ANC contacts to reduce perinatal mortality and improve women’s care experiences. These guidelines also recommend TTCV vaccination for all pregnant women, depending on their previous tetanus vaccination exposure, to prevent neonatal mortality from tetanus. 8. Integrating TTCV into ANC is a sustainable way to ensure pregnant women are protected against tetanus. In the long term, ensuring that everyone receives the full infant TTCV series and required booster doses will provide lifelong protection against tetanus. 9. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a leading cause of liver cancer and liver disease. In 2015, an estimated 257 million people were living with chronic HBV infection, and approximately 887,220 deaths were attributed to HBV infection. 10. Perinatal transmission or early childhood exposure are significant causes of chronic hepatitis B infection. WHO recommends that all infants, including those with low birth weight and premature infants, receive their first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, ideally within 24 hours. 11. Despite this recommendation, the integration of the hepatitis B birth dose (HepB-BD) as a standard component of quality newborn care is not universally adopted. National policies or local practices in some countries do not support its implementation. For instance, many babies born at home may not have timely access to vaccination. 12. The delivery of HepB-BD differs from other vaccinations because it cannot be scheduled, requiring the health system to respond within 24 hours of childbirth. Successful delivery of HepB-BD necessitates integration with maternal and newborn care in health facilities or through home visits. 13. Strategic integration of HepB-BD should be tailored to the local context, focusing on the number of home births and the training of health workers responsible for administering the vaccine. Vaccinating newborns with HepB-BD at health facilities and during home visits has demonstrated additional benefits, such as earlier birth registration and the provision of other postnatal care. 14. A project in India’s Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh states operationalized an existing strategy to vaccinate newborns with HepB-BD, oral polio vaccine birth dose, and Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG). Results showed that vaccinating newborns at health facilities shortly after birth was feasible and replicable. Additionally, early birth registration in health-facility records facilitated subsequent follow-up for complete immunization and other services. 15. Using a standardized checklist, healthcare providers identified each beneficiary’s needs and provided services either during the same visit or through referrals. Providers in immunization, newborn care, and pediatric/sick baby units were trained to improve interpersonal communication, counseling skills, and systematic postpartum screening. 16. The checklist emphasized screening or referral for services such as postnatal care (PNC) for women who delivered within six weeks, lactational amenorrhea method (LAM) counseling, postpartum family planning (PPFP), immunization for children under five years old, and other additional services as needed. 17. Beneficiaries attending immunization, newborn care, and pediatric services were more likely to be screened for family planning, postnatal care, and immunization services when the postpartum systematic screening checklist was used. 18. Before integrating an immunization program with other interventions, several criteria should be considered, including the target group, timing, logistical requirements, and acceptability among patients, communities, and health workers. Additionally, the health system context, such as political will, national policies, financial support, and primary healthcare structures, must be evaluated. 19. The compatibility of potential services for integration should be assessed, focusing on target populations, intervention types, timing of service delivery, logistical needs, health-worker training, stakeholder support, costs, and supply-chain requirements. 20. Examples from Uganda and Kenya highlight the importance of tailoring integration strategies to local contexts. In Uganda, the schistosomiasis control program used National Immunization Days to reach target populations. In Kenya, providing hygiene kits alongside vaccination services increased vaccine coverage in urban settings but was insufficient to overcome access barriers in rural areas.
